clue.text: Stone dust described by Eliza Cook and Anita Desai

definitions.text: dust described by Eliza Cook and Anita Desai

explanation.surface: A literary note on gem dust as written about by two women authors.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition names the word that goes before 'dust': Eliza Cook wrote a poem called 'Diamond Dust', and Anita Desai a story collection of the same title.
explanation.definitionFit: A diamond is a precious stone, and 'Diamond Dust' is the title both writers used.

clue.text: New Credo stir from board members

indicators.note: making something new out of the letters signals that they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fresh statement of belief stirs up the company's board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' points to rearranging the nine letters of CREDO STIR; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Company directors are the people who sit on its board.

clue.text: Foot of a North American troublemaker

parts.note: a pest is a nuisance or troublemaker

explanation.surface: The foot belonging to an irritating person from North America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' is the poetic sense: a metrical unit, here the one spelt this way in American usage (anapaest in British spelling).
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody a metrical foot of two short syllables followed by a long one.

clue.text: "… all patience, and impatience; / All purity, all trial, all —" (As You Like It)

definitions.text: "… all patience, and impatience; / All purity, all trial, all —" (As You Like It)

parts.words: "… all patience, and impatience; / All purity, all trial, all —" (As You Like It)
parts.note: a quotation with its final word missing: Silvius's list in Act 5 of what it is to love ends on a word for humble deference

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the blank: in As You Like It (5.2) Silvius's speech runs 'All humbleness, all patience and impatience, All purity, all trial, all observance', which some editions print with this word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means deferential respect or homage, fitting a lover's list of devotions.

clue.text: Sort of art in home-made colours

indicators.note: the answer is found sitting in the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: A kind of artwork painted with homemade paints.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'home-maDE COlours'.
explanation.definitionFit: Art Deco is the 1920s-30s decorative style, so it is a sort of art.

clue.text: Implied American historian

parts.note: tacit means understood or implied without being stated

explanation.surface: An American historian whose meaning is only hinted at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Implied' looks like a verb but is the adjective TACIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author of the Annals and Histories was a historian.

clue.text: Location of cheaper seats for Genet production

explanation.surface: Where the cheap seats are for a staging of a Genet play.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper-tier theatre seating is usually cheaper, and Jean Genet wrote a play with this title (Le Balcon).

clue.text: Percy Lubbock's fictional vessel?

parts.note: Lubbock wrote a classic study of the novelist's skill, The ___ of Fiction; the same word also means a boat

explanation.surface: A ship that appears in a novel by Percy Lubbock.
explanation.walkthrough: Lubbock's book is 'The Craft of Fiction' (1921), a critical study, not a novel; 'fictional' joins the title word to 'Fiction', and 'vessel' gives the boat sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A craft is a boat or ship, and it is also skill, the subject of Lubbock's study.

clue.text: Eight-line verse (though a threesome is allowed)

parts.note: a trio is a group of three
let means to permit, as in 'let in'

explanation.surface: A short poem of eight lines, even though a group of three is permitted.
explanation.definitionFit: A triolet is a fixed poetic form of eight lines with repeated refrains.

clue.text: Elinor Dashwood personified it

parts.note: in Austen's novel the elder sister stands for one half of its title, the half opposed to her sister's sensibility

explanation.surface: A character from Jane Austen embodied some quality.
explanation.walkthrough: In Jane Austen's 'Sense and Sensibility' Elinor is the prudent sister and Marianne the emotional one.
explanation.definitionFit: Elinor represents good judgment and prudence, the first quality in Austen's title.

clue.text: Novelist who made hard cash

parts.note: the Victorian writer of The Cloister and the Hearth also wrote a novel titled Hard Cash

explanation.surface: A writer who earned real money.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade (1814-84) wrote 'Hard Cash' (1863); 'made hard cash' reads as getting rich but means writing that book.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist whose works include Hard Cash.

clue.text: Son of general and queen gets a raise somehow in swindle

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are placed in the word for swindle

parts.note: a con is a swindle

indicators.note: somehow says the letters come out in some other order

explanation.surface: A child of a commander and a monarch gets a pay rise through fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges A RAISE to AESARI, and 'in' puts that inside CON.
explanation.definitionFit: Ptolemy XV was the son of Julius Caesar, a Roman general, and Cleopatra, queen of Egypt.

clue.text: Sir Edward, rather crumpled English historian?

definitions.text: Sir Edward, rather crumpled English historian?

parts.words: Sir Edward, rather crumpled English historian?
parts.note: the surname of a Victorian historian knighted as Sir Edward is also an adjective meaning full of folds

explanation.surface: A slightly rumpled English historian with a knighthood.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edward Creasy wrote 'The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World' (1851); his surname also reads as 'full of creases'.
explanation.definitionFit: The historian's surname doubles as the adjective for wrinkled or crumpled cloth.

clue.text: Sir John gets off least unfavourably

indicators.note: the letters are set out unfavourably, in a disordered arrangement

explanation.surface: A knight gets away with the lightest punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' is a link; 'unfavourably' signals rearranging OFF LEAST. 'gets off least' looks like a phrase about escaping punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Fastolf was the English knight of the Hundred Years War, linked with Shakespeare's Falstaff.

clue.text: May a book's second one bring about a change of view?

definitions.text: May a book's second one bring about a change of view?

parts.words: May a book's second one bring about a change of view?
parts.note: a reprinting of a book is called by the same word as the opinion it leaves on a reader

explanation.surface: Could a book's second reading make you change your mind?
explanation.walkthrough: A 'second impression' is a reprint; a second impression of someone is a revised opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: A printing run of a book and the idea a thing gives you share one word.

clue.text: Some support (only a little ) for playwright

indicators.note: only some of these letters are taken, the run sitting across two words

explanation.surface: A dramatist gets a small amount of backing.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'suppORT ONly'; '(only a little)' backs up the idea of taking just part.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Orton was an English playwright, author of Loot and Entertaining Mr Sloane.

clue.text: His Drama was first seen in 1940, his Theatre did not appear until 1954

definitions.text: His Drama was first seen in 1940, his Theatre did not appear until 1954

parts.words: His Drama was first seen in 1940, his Theatre did not appear until 1954
parts.note: two books of theatre criticism, Drama and Theatre, published fourteen years apart by one British critic

explanation.surface: Reads like a stage career, with a play opening and a playhouse built years later.
explanation.walkthrough: Desmond MacCarthy, drama critic of the New Statesman, collected his reviews as 'Drama' (1940) and 'Theatre' (1954); 'first seen' and 'did not appear' sound like stage openings.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Desmond MacCarthy published the critical collections Drama and Theatre in those years.

clue.text: Unusual satire, with new pep, supplies foretaste

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters appear in an unusual order
new says the following word is itself to be made over, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd piece of satire, freshly energised, gives a hint of what is to come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' and 'Unusual' both signal rearrangement: SATIRE plus PEP give the nine letters. The definition needs 'supplies' to read 'what supplies a foretaste'.
explanation.definitionFit: A starter dish gives a small taste ahead of the main meal.

clue.text: Terminal award-winner

parts.note: an American dramatist won an Obie award for a 1969 play called Terminal

explanation.surface: Someone who wins a prize at the very end.
explanation.walkthrough: Susan Yankowitz wrote 'Terminal' (1969) for the Open Theater; 'Terminal' looks like an adjective (final, fatal) but is the play's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan Yankowitz is the playwright whose Terminal won an Obie.

clue.text: Supreme council hardens in modified form

indicators.note: the letters are given in a modified form, meaning rearranged

explanation.surface: A ruling body takes a firmer line in a revised shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' belongs to the fodder: HARDENS IN rearranged; 'modified form' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest Jewish court and legislative assembly in ancient Jerusalem.

clue.text: Knight with broken heart gets kiss in portico

parts.note: N is the chess notation for knight

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the word are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: X is the conventional kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A heartbroken knight is kissed under a church porch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges HEART to ARTHE, between N and X.
explanation.definitionFit: A narthex is the entrance porch or vestibule at the west end of a church.

clue.text: Heathen, like Edna O'Brien's place?

explanation.surface: A non-believer, as in the setting of an Irish novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Edna O'Brien's novel is 'A Pagan Place' (1970).
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is a non-Christian, and O'Brien's title describes such a place.

clue.text: Language from Antigua ran into difficulties

indicators.note: the letters are taken from the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone from a Caribbean island got into trouble with their speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'antiGUA RAN Into'; the anagram-looking 'difficulties' only completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Guarani is an indigenous language widely spoken in Paraguay.

clue.text: Poem good Italians might eventually aspire to, perhaps

definitions.text: Poem good Italians might eventually aspire to, perhaps

parts.words: Poem good Italians might eventually aspire to, perhaps
parts.note: the third part of Dante's Divine Comedy is named after heaven, where the good hope to end up

explanation.surface: A poem that virtuous Italians might hope to reach.
explanation.walkthrough: Dante's 'Divine Comedy' ends in heaven, the 'Paradiso'; 'eventually' is the afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: The final canticle of Dante's poem depicts heaven, the goal of the virtuous.

clue.text: Some of Shaw's were unpleasant

parts.note: Shaw grouped early dramas under a title pairing them as Pleasant and Unpleasant

explanation.surface: Some of George Bernard Shaw's work was disagreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw published 'Plays Pleasant and Plays Unpleasant' (1898); the clue reads as a slight on Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's dramatic works are his stage works, some collected as Unpleasant.

clue.text: Bagworthy giant, achieved nothing inside

indicators.note: inside puts the letter for nothing within the word for achieved

parts.note: done means achieved or completed
O, the zero shape, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A huge man from Bagworthy did nothing indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Carver Doone is the giant villain of R. D. Blackmore's 'Lorna Doone', whose outlaw family live in Bagworthy (Badgworthy) on Exmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: Carver Doone, of the outlaw clan in Lorna Doone, is a man of huge size.

clue.text: Street artist with personal problem as Greek historian

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword artist
BO, body odour, is the classic personal problem

explanation.surface: A street painter with a hygiene issue posing as an ancient writer.
explanation.walkthrough: BO is body odour, a stock euphemism for a 'personal problem'; RA is a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Strabo was a Greek geographer and historian of the first century.

clue.text: Net mention for novelist

indicators.note: mention means the word is said out loud, so we go by sound

parts.note: a web is a net or mesh

explanation.surface: Bringing up the internet for a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Webb wrote 'Precious Bane'; 'Net' looks like the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Webb was an English novelist of Shropshire life.

clue.text: Black hairstyle, say, tied differently for goddess

indicators.note: say means we take the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: an Afro is a rounded hairstyle associated with Black people

indicators.note: differently means the letters are arranged in another way

explanation.surface: A goddess wears an Afro, tied up in a new style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives the sound of AFRO, spelt APHRO; 'differently' rearranges TIED to DITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphrodite is the Greek goddess of love.

clue.text: R. K. Narayan's teacher took to the water with me

parts.note: swam means went swimming, took to the water
I is the speaker, me

explanation.surface: An Indian novelist's teacher went swimming with me.
explanation.walkthrough: Narayan's first novel is 'Swami and Friends'; Swami is the schoolboy hero, but a swami is a Hindu religious teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A swami is a Hindu religious teacher, and Swami is Narayan's title character.

clue.text: "At — you departed, / You went into Ku-to yen" (Ezra Pound)

definitions.text: "At — you departed, / You went into Ku-to yen" (Ezra Pound)

parts.words: "At — you departed, / You went into Ku-to yen" (Ezra Pound)
parts.note: a quotation from Pound's The River-Merchant's Wife with an age missing

explanation.surface: Lines from Ezra Pound with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the blank from Pound's 'The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter', after Li Po: the wife's husband left when she was this age.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is an age in years, a number one more than fifteen.

clue.text: French composer shows love for model in language school

indicators.note: for means one letter takes the place of another

parts.note: Berlitz is a well-known chain of language schools
T, as in the Ford Model T
O is love, the zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: A French composer swaps romance for a mannequin at a language college.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'shows love for model in language school': O replaces T inside BERLITZ.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector Berlioz was a French Romantic composer of the Symphonie fantastique.
